or_north_face_3.blurb: The North Face is the wall of Broughton Bluff that looks out toward the Columbia River and can be spotted from the interstate, a short drive east of Portland. It holds about a dozen mostly traditional lines on basalt, with a couple of bolted ones, running from easy fifth-class up to low 5.13. Most of the grades cluster around 5.9, so it suits climbers comfortable on moderate gear routes. Several of the best lines go in multiple pitches, which gives it a bigger feel than the single-pitch walls around it. Come equipped with a trad rack and an eye on the weather, since the bluff tends to hold dampness through winter.

or_poison_oak_wall.blurb: Poison Oak Wall is a short cliff above the trail at Emigrant Lake, just outside Ashland in southern Oregon. Walls here are roughly 60 to 70 feet, and most of the dozen lines are bolted sport routes with fixed anchors, plus a single trad line, one top rope and a boulder problem. Grades start at very easy and rise to the low 5.11s, with the bulk in the easy to moderate range, which makes it a friendly spot for a first lead or for setting up top ropes. As the name warns, poison oak grows thick around the base, so long clothes help, especially outside winter.

or_n_snake_rock.blurb: Snake Rock sits on the quieter west side of Smith Rock State Park, away from the crowds of the main canyon. About a dozen climbs are spread across it, nine bolted and three on gear, from 5.8 up into the 5.13 range, with a fairly even mix of moderate and hard lines. A sharp arete marks the middle of the wall. The cliff gets shade through the morning and picks up sun in the afternoon, and a few lines stay shaded the whole day, which helps in warm weather. Reaching it takes a real hike or scramble from the main park.
or_n_snake_rock.approach: Three ways in: scramble over Asterisk Pass, go over Misery Ridge and turn upriver, or loop around the southern tip of the park and climb up to the pass. A rope is advised for the pass scramble.

or_valhalla.blurb: Valhalla is a steep, bowl-shaped crag in the Terra Nova area of southwest Oregon, set behind several better-known formations. All twelve routes are single-pitch sport lines, and the layout makes it a good place to rig top ropes, since you arrive at the anchors on top and lower or rappel in. Grades go from 5.7 to 5.11, though the weight sits at 5.10 and 5.11, so it is more of an intermediate crag than a beginner one. The climb out of the bowl after a session is a workout of its own.
or_valhalla.approach: Hike uphill past Bird Rock and the highball boulders on top of that formation, then follow the developed trail to the anchors on top of Valhalla and drop in from there.

or_a_dreamland.blurb: Dreamland is the leftmost section of Marsupial Wall, on the far side of the gorge from the main face of Smith Rock. The wall here turns to look northwest, and the climbing is steep, all bolted sport, with built-out terraces at the base. Twelve routes run from 5.10 into the 5.13s, and most of them are 5.12 or 5.13, so it is a place for strong, experienced leaders rather than newcomers. Expect a long hike in, roughly an hour, and few other people once you arrive.

or_j_rope_de_dope_block.blurb: Rope de Dope Block is a lone, solid cube about 40 feet tall that stands beside the canyon trail at Smith Rock, before the footbridge over the river. Almost everything here is bolted and easy to reach, with one crack for gear. Grades run from 5.5 to 5.10, with most lines at 5.9 and 5.10, so it works for newer leaders and for top-rope practice. The top is reached by a short, bouldery scramble up the back side. Shade lasts through most of the day, and the block draws guided classes, scout groups and families.
or_j_rope_de_dope_block.approach: Take the main canyon trail down from the lot and, before the river crossing, bear left and walk a short way, around a quarter mile, to the block.
